title: Bosonic quantum control with a weakly coupled fluxonium qubit
authors: Anaida Ali, Shantanu R. Jha, Shoumik D. Chowdhury, Lev-Arcady Sellem, Max Hays, William D. Oliver, Baptiste Royer
abstract: Echoed Conditional Displacement (ECD) gates constitute a fundamental building block for quantum control of harmonic oscillator modes. However, bit-flips of the auxiliary qubit remain a dominant error mechanism for this kind of bosonic control. In this work, we present a numerical case study of a bit-flip protected fluxonium operating as the control qubit and numerically implement ECD gates in a single-mode resonator-fluxonium device, demonstrating that fidelities exceeding 99.9% are possible. We systematically investigate the resonator dynamics using a combination of semiclassical trajectories and master equation simulations, numerically revealing asymptotic saturation of the dispersive shift in the strongly driven regime of the resonator. We develop an efficient technique to numerically simulate the strongly driven regime of the resonator using a semiclassical formulation that maps the full perturbation series in the dispersive expansion as order-by-order frequency shifts. This provides a compact polynomial description of the resonator which is intuitive and remains valid throughout the dispersive regime. Furthermore, we propose an improved ECD sequence that accounts for the effects of photon loss and spurious nonlinear terms on resonator trajectories.
summary: This paper presents a detailed numerical study on implementing high-fidelity quantum gates, specifically ECD gates, in a resonator coupled to a fluxonium qubit. By utilizing the fluxonium's inherent protection against bit-flips and developing advanced simulation techniques, the authors achieve fidelities over 99.9%. The work is significant for advancing practical quantum control in superconducting circuit platforms.
main_problem: The work addresses the challenge of achieving high-fidelity quantum control for bosonic modes, specifically by implementing Echoed Conditional Displacement (ECD) gates while mitigating dominant error sources like qubit bit-flips and resonator nonlinearities.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that fidelities exceeding 99.9% are achievable for ECD gates using a fluxonium qubit protected at the half-flux sweet spot, and they propose an improved sequence to counteract photon loss and nonlinearities.
method: The study combines numerical case studies, semiclassical trajectory simulations, and master equation approaches to model the coupled resonator-fluxonium system dynamics.
model_or_system: The system is a single-mode resonator coupled to a fluxonium qubit. The Hamiltonian is analyzed in various frames (dispersive, displaced) and includes terms up to sixth order, requiring advanced simulation techniques to handle strong driving and dissipation.
key_observables: Gate fidelities (exceeding 99.9%), resonator dynamics (dispersive shift saturation), and vacuum overlap for the ECD gate.
important_parameters: Operating the fluxonium at the half-flux sweet spot ($\Phi_e = \Phi_0/2$), and the strong driving regime ($\langle\hat{a}^\dagger\hat{a}angle\gg 1$).
main_assumptions: The standard ECD sequence is limited by qubit bit-flips, which is mitigated by using the fluxonium; the analysis relies on semiclassical approximations for strong driving.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the out-and-back protocol for parameter extraction, the vacuum overlap of the ECD return state, and comparisons showing fidelity improvements using the modified ECD sequence and repumping protocols.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for high-fidelity bosonic control (ECD gates) to developing advanced simulation techniques for the strongly driven regime, deriving an improved gate sequence to handle losses, and finally demonstrating high-fidelity operation using repumping protocols.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles practical limitations (dissipation, nonlinearities) in implementing fundamental quantum gates for bosonic modes, which is a core area of quantum optics and quantum information.
